newsitem.title: UK: NatWest outlook grim, analysts cut forecasts.
newsitem.headline: NatWest outlook grim, analysts cut forecasts.

text.p: Banking analysts continued to cut their profit forecasts for National Westminster Bank Plc on Tuesday in the aftermath of the departure of its investment banking chief and a first half profits warning.
They were also less than complimentary about the bank's near-term prospects with Robert Law of Lehman Brothers stating that even the most radical action might not transform the bank's prospects.

"NatWest looks set for a long haul," Law said in a research note. "It is difficult to escape the conclusion that NatWest has no obviously sizeable businesses with attractive profitability, market share or competitive advantage."

On Monday, NatWest announced that Martin Owen, who has run NatWest Markets since 1992, was resigning and warned that the group will make no more than 770 million pounds ($1.3 billion) in the first half of this year -- substantially lower than some had expected.
Law cut his 1996 profit forecast by 13 percent to 1.75 billion pounds from 2.0 billion and now sees 2.0 billion in 1998, cut from a previous estimate of 2.3 billion.
Analysts had already been trimming their forecasts before Monday's dramatic events as they had been receiving briefings from the company ahead of the release of half-year figures in August.

Nick Collier of Morgan Stanley said he had downgraded his forecast to 1.788 billion stg for the full year from 2.043 billion before Monday's news and stressed he was still hoping for greater clarity from NatWest's management.

Chief executive Derek Wanless, who is temporarily taking over at NatWest Markets, and chairman Lord Alexander are now under intense pressure to turn the business round and prove to the market and institutional shareholders that they regard shareholder value of paramount importance.

"They have to be clearer on the strategy both for themselves and for the investor community," Collier said, adding that NatWest markets needs to concentrate on those areas where it has a competitive advantage such as its Treasury operation where the bank has a dominant position with UK corporate clients.
John Leonard, banking analyst at Salomon Brothers said he had reduced his forecast for this year to 1.765 billion pounds from 1.825 billion.

Leonard said he was disappointed that Monday's announcement had not included the name of the new NatWest Markets chief and said that an internal appointment would signal to him the likelihood of a less ambitious strategy.
"One thing you can't do in this business is drift," Leonard said.

The downgrades continued with UBS cutting to 1.725 billion pounds this year from 2.150 but analyst John Aitken, who met NatWest management after its announcement on Monday, took "significant consolation" from the possibility that NatWest will pursue a less expansionary investment banking strategy.

"We understand that while NatWest 'remains committed to investment banking', there is likely to be much greater focus on key product and geographic areas and on improving returns in the short-term," Aitken said in a research note on Tuesday.
Aitken added that investors may think a poor set of interim results will be an acceptable trade-off for a smaller and more profitable investment bank.

Press reports speculated that NatWest would withdraw from various aspects of investment banking but a spokeswoman said on Tuesday that it was not pulling out of Eurobonds and had said nothing about cutting staff numbers.

Amid continued scepticism that NatWest has sorted out its strategy, UBS's Aitken, who remains an "unhappy" buyer of the stock, seemed to sum up the feelings of the market as NatWest's shares dropped a further 10p to 745p.

"There has been an appalling catalogue of errors and underperformance," said Aitken, "but if this kicks NatWest into downsizing investment banking and paying more attention to getting an early improvement in performance, then it is some consolation."
